passage: At the end of our marketing project, our professor did something sneaky. She asked each of the four of us, privately, to write what percentage of the work we had done. I wrote 45%, and honestly I thought I was being modest. I had stayed up all night for the final deck. Then she read out the numbers. Zeenat, 40%. Kiran, 50%. Tushar, 55%. Me, 45%. That's 190% of one project. Zeenat laughed first. "Samir, you remember the deck. I remember the survey I ran for two weeks." She was right; I'd barely noticed the survey. Each of us had seen our own late nights up close and everyone else's from far away. On the next project, we kept a shared log of who did what, with dates.

qa.q: What percentage did Samir write?
Why did Samir think 45% was modest?
qa.a: Samir felt proud of staying up all night for the final deck, and that night felt so big that 45% seemed a modest share.

qa.q: What did the team do on the next project, and why does it help?
qa.a: They kept a shared, dated log of who did what, so credit rests on a record rather than on each person's memory.

qa.q: How did Zeenat see the 190% total?
qa.a: Zeenat found it funny and pointed out that each of them remembered their own work, like her two-week survey, more than anyone else's.

grounding: A student recalls a team whose private estimates of their own share added up to 190%, and how a shared log fixed it.

passage:
Project guide's note, final-year mechanical projects, 20 April
During today's viva, Thomas and Uday each told me separately that they had built most of the solar dryer. Thomas said he "did the whole frame and all the calculations." Uday said he "designed it and handled the frame welding." Both were sincere; neither was lying on purpose. When I asked for their work logs, they had none. From the photos on their phones, it looks as though Thomas did most of the calculations and Uday most of the welding, and each remembers his own part as the bigger one. I have asked both to write a dated list of tasks from their messages and photos before marks are finalised. From next year, I will ask every team to keep a weekly log from day one.

qa.q: What did Thomas say he did?
qa.a: The whole frame and all the calculations.

qa.q: Why might Thomas and Uday both sincerely believe they did most of the work?
qa.a: Each felt proud of his own long hours, which he remembers up close, while the other's work seemed smaller from a distance.

qa.q: What is the guide asking for, and why is it fair?
qa.a: A dated task list from messages and photos, and weekly logs next year, so recognition rests on records rather than memory.

qa.q: How might Uday feel when he hears Thomas's claim?
qa.a: Uday might feel hurt or annoyed, since he remembers designing it and doing the welding himself.

grounding: A project guide records two students each sincerely claiming most of the work, and asks for dated records to settle credit.

passage:
Friday, hostel
Presentation done. We got an A. And honestly? That was mostly me. I did the research, the slides AND I presented. Uday just did "the data," whatever that was.
Later, in the mess, I heard Uday tell Nitin he had "carried the whole thing," because he spent three nights cleaning the survey data. Three nights? I didn't even know that took three nights. I was annoyed at first. Then I tried adding it up: if he thinks he did 70% and I think I did 70%, that's 140%. We can't both be right.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask him to go through our chat history with me and write down who did what. Next time, a shared list from day one.

passage:
Dear Yusuf,
Now that the school-library grant has come through, I want to thank you properly and also be honest about how it happened.
What I did well: I wrote the proposal, and I think the story of the Class 5 reading club was strong.
What luck did: the foundation had extra money this year because another project dropped out. We might not have been funded otherwise.
What I got wrong: I missed the error on the budget page, and you caught it at 11 p.m. the night before. Without that, we'd have been rejected on a technicality.
And you: the photos, the parents' letters, and that late-night catch. I'll say all of this in Monday's meeting too.
Thank you.
Bhavna

qa.q: Why did the foundation have extra money this year?
qa.a: Because another project dropped out.

qa.q: What does Bhavna seem to feel toward Yusuf?
qa.a: Bhavna feels grateful, thanking Yusuf for the photos, the parents' letters and the late-night catch.

qa.q: Why is Bhavna's three-part account useful?
qa.a: Naming what went well, what luck helped and what went wrong gives an honest picture, so the team can learn and trust the credit.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel hearing this in Monday's meeting?
qa.a: Yusuf would probably feel valued and respected, since Yusuf's catch is named in front of everyone rather than forgotten.

grounding: A young professional credits their own work, names the luck and a mistake, and thanks a colleague honestly after a grant success.

passage: Vishal, when you asked on this show how our clinic cut its waiting times, people expect the story where Elizabeth is the hero. Here's the honest one. I did some things well: I mapped every step a patient takes, and I pushed for the token system. But luck helped: the new receptionist joined that month and happened to be brilliant with the software. And I got things wrong: I first blamed the doctors for delays, when really it was files going missing between rooms. The nurses spotted that, not me. So the thanks go to Sister Mary's team and to our receptionist, Anil. I'm proud of my part. It just wasn't the whole thing.

qa.q: What was really causing the delays?
qa.a: Files going missing between rooms.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth feel about the part played?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels proud of mapping the steps and pushing the token system, but honest that it wasn't the whole thing.

qa.q: What makes Elizabeth's account a fair way to own results?
qa.a: It names Elizabeth's own contribution, the luck of a brilliant receptionist and the mistake about the doctors, and thanks the people who found the real cause.

qa.q: How might Sister Mary's team feel hearing this?
qa.a: They would probably feel recognised and appreciated, since their discovery about the files is credited.

grounding: A young professional describes a success by naming their own part, the luck involved and a mistake, and thanking others.

passage: I was at the back of the hall when Uma gave her speech after the flood-relief drive, so I heard every word. We'd collected more supplies than any college in the district, and everyone expected her to take a bow. Instead she said, "Three things. I planned the collection points well; I'm proud of that. We were lucky: a local paper wrote about us on day two, and donations tripled. And I made a mistake: I forgot to arrange trucks, and Rehana's uncle lent us his for free." Then she thanked the volunteers by name, all thirty-one of them. I watched her face while she read the names. I can't say what she was feeling, but she didn't rush a single one.

qa.q: How many volunteers did Uma thank by name?
qa.a: All thirty-one.

qa.q: What might Uma's slow reading of the names suggest?
qa.a: She probably felt genuinely grateful to each volunteer, taking care not to rush anyone.

qa.q: Why is Uma's three-part speech a good way to own a success?
qa.a: She credited her planning, admitted the lucky newspaper story and her truck mistake, and thanked others, which builds trust.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel hearing the uncle's truck mentioned?
qa.a: Rehana would probably feel pleased and proud that the family's help was named in front of everyone.

grounding: A volunteer describes a young woman owning a success fairly by naming her part, the luck and her mistake, and thanking everyone.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Wednesday, after assembly
At the water cooler this morning, Kunal and Ankita both pushed in the line, a few minutes apart. When I spoke to Kunal, he said, "I only pushed because the bell was ringing and I was late for PE." Ten minutes later, when Ankita pushed him, he came to me red-faced: "Ankita pushed me because she's rude. She's always rude." When I asked whether Ankita might have been in a hurry too, he said, "No, she's just like that." I asked him to think about what he had told me about the bell. He was quiet, then said, "Maybe she had PE too." Both children apologised. I will talk to the class about queues on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Kunal say he pushed?
qa.a: Because the bell was ringing and he was late for PE.

qa.q: Why did Kunal think Ankita pushed because she is rude?
qa.a: He felt upset and hurt at being pushed, so it seemed like her character, while his own push felt like it had a good reason.

qa.q: What question did the teacher ask that helped, and why?
qa.a: Whether Ankita might have been in a hurry too, which reminded Kunal of his own bell reason so he could see she might have one.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel being called always rude?
qa.a: Ankita might feel hurt and unfairly labelled, especially if she was rushing too.

grounding: A teacher records a boy explaining his own push by the bell but another child's push by rudeness.

passage:
Sunday
Vidya didi shouted at me today for using her headphones. She is SO rude. She's always rude when I just ask for something.
Okay, I didn't ask. I just took them. But still.
Then in the evening I shouted at her when she came into my room, because I was tired from cricket practice and my knee hurt. That's different. I had a reason.
Mummy said, "Maybe Vidya had a reason too. She has boards tomorrow." I forgot about her boards.
So when I shout it's because I'm tired, and when she shouts it's because she's rude? Hmm. That doesn't seem fair when I write it down.
Hemant

qa.q: Why did Hemant shout at Vidya in the evening?
qa.a: Because Hemant was tired from cricket practice and the knee hurt.

qa.q: Why did Hemant decide Vidya is rude?
qa.a: Hemant felt hurt at being shouted at and didn't think about her boards, so it seemed like her character rather than her stress.

qa.q: What could Hemant do next time before calling someone rude?
qa.a: Ask, as Mummy did, whether they might have a reason too, like the reasons Hemant has for shouting.

qa.q: What might Vidya's day have been like?
qa.a: Vidya had boards the next day, so she was probably stressed, and her headphones had been taken without asking.

grounding: A child's diary shows excusing their own shouting as tiredness while calling a sister's shouting rudeness.

passage: At the Dussehra mela beside the village tank, the queue for the giant wheel was long and hot. Vijay's father had given him exactly one ticket and told him to be back by six for the Ravan burning. At 5:40 Vijay pushed past two boys to get ahead. "I have to be back by six," he muttered. "It's not my fault." Five minutes later, Akash from the next village elbowed past him too. "Hey!" Vijay shouted. "Bully! You think you own the queue!" Akash turned, panting. "My little sister is lost near the sweet stalls. I'm going to the loudspeaker man." Vijay stepped back and watched him run, suddenly aware of his own elbows.

qa.q: What time did Vijay have to be back?
qa.a: By six, for the Ravan burning.

qa.q: Why did Vijay call Akash a bully?
qa.a: He felt angry at being elbowed, so it seemed like Akash's nature, while his own pushing felt excused by the six o'clock deadline.

qa.q: What could Vijay learn from Akash's answer?
qa.a: That other people who push may have urgent reasons too, like a lost sister, just as Vijay had his deadline.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling as he pushed past?
qa.a: Akash was probably frightened and desperate, running to the loudspeaker man because his little sister was lost.

grounding: A boy excuses his own pushing at a fair by his deadline but calls another boy a bully, until he hears the boy's reason.

passage: At dinner in their Nairobi flat, Daniel's phone buzzed for the fifth time, and his mother, Wanjiru, reached over and turned it face down. "Not at the table." Daniel snapped. "You always have to control everything!" He stormed to his room and slammed the door. Lying on his bed, he told himself he hadn't really been shouting; he was just stressed about the chemistry test tomorrow and the group chat arguing about it. Mum, on the other hand, just liked being in charge. In the kitchen, Wanjiru scraped the plates, telling herself she hadn't really been angry. She was exhausted from a double shift at the hospital and just wanted one quiet meal. Daniel, obviously, had simply become rude. Neither of them knew about the other's day.

qa.q: What was Daniel stressed about?
qa.a: The chemistry test tomorrow and the group chat arguing about it.

qa.q: Why did Daniel feel his own snapping was different from his mother's?
qa.a: He felt stressed and saw his outburst as caused by the test, while he saw his mother's action as her wanting control.

qa.q: What small step could help Daniel and Wanjiru after the argument?
qa.a: Each could say what their day was like, the test and the double shift, before judging the other's character.

qa.q: How does Wanjiru see Daniel's shouting?
qa.a: Wanjiru sees it as Daniel becoming rude, not knowing about his test stress, while she excuses her own reaction as exhaustion.

grounding: A teenage boy explains his outburst as stress and his mother's as control, while she explains hers as tiredness and his as rudeness.

passage: On visiting day at the boarding school, Siddharth's father arrived with a tiffin of rajma and the report card already in his hand. Within five minutes they were shouting in a corner of the visitors' hall. "You're not even trying!" "You never listen!" Later, back in the dorm, Siddharth told his friend Eshaan, "I only shouted because I'm stressed. Exams, hostel food, no sleep. He shouted because he just wants to control me." Eshaan, who had watched from the next bench, said slowly, "Your dad left home at four in the morning to get here. He kept checking the bus timetable the whole time you talked." Siddharth paused. "He didn't say that." "You didn't tell him about the exams either," Eshaan said. "He probably thinks you're just being rude."

qa.q: What time did Siddharth's father leave home?
qa.a: At four in the morning.

qa.q: Why does Siddharth feel his own shouting was different from his father's?
qa.a: He feels it came from stress about exams, hostel food and no sleep, while his father's shouting seems to him like a wish to control.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do at the next visit?
qa.a: Tell his father about the exam stress and ask about the journey, so each understands the other's pressures.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's father see the argument?
qa.a: He probably thinks Siddharth was just being rude, not knowing about the stress, while his own shouting came from worry and a long, tiring journey.

grounding: At a boarding school visit, a teenage boy blames his own shouting on stress and his father's on control, missing his father's situation.

passage:

passage:
Monday. Irfan didn't show up for the lab session they had booked together, and Irawati had to run the whole experiment alone. She fumed all evening. "He's selfish," she wrote. "He only cares about his own marks."
Wednesday. Still angry, Irawati tried something her counsellor had once suggested. She wrote the story as if it had happened to her friend Mitali: "Mitali's lab partner didn't come. What might explain it?" Written that way, she thought of three reasons in a minute: sick, family, a clash. Then she wrote it from Irfan's seat: "I missed the lab and couldn't message because..." She stopped. She didn't know.
Friday. She asked him. His scholarship interview had been moved to Monday morning with one day's notice, and his phone had died in the waiting room. "I should have found a way to tell you," he said. "I should have asked," she said.

qa.q: Why did Irfan miss the lab?
qa.a: His scholarship interview was moved to Monday morning with one day's notice, and his phone died in the waiting room.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling on Monday evening?
qa.a: She felt angry and let down, fuming that Irfan was selfish after she ran the experiment alone.

qa.q: What technique helped Irawati, and why?
qa.a: Writing the incident as a friend's story and then from Irfan's seat, which made situational reasons easier to see and led her to ask him.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel when Irawati asks instead of accusing?
qa.a: Irfan probably feels relieved and a bit guilty, ready to admit he should have found a way to tell her.

grounding: Over a week, a student in conflict rewrites the incident as a friend's story and from the other person's seat, and finds reasons on both sides.

passage: Darshan, you're furious with your roommate, I can see it. Let your Yamini atya tell you how I handled mine when I was twenty. Her name was Kokila, and she played music until 1 a.m. every night before my exams. I decided she was the most selfish girl in Pune. Then my warden gave me a strange task: "Write what happened as if it were your friend's story. Then write it from Kokila's bed." The first version made me laugh; I'd have told my friend, "Just talk to her." The second was harder. From her bed, I realised she worked evenings at a bakery, and the music was the only way she could stay awake to study. Next day we made a deal: headphones for her, earplugs for me.

qa.q: Where did Kokila work in the evenings?
qa.a: At a bakery.

qa.q: What was young Yamini feeling about Kokila at first?
qa.a: She felt angry and resentful, deciding Kokila was the most selfish girl in Pune for playing music before her exams.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: The warden's task of writing it as a friend's story and from Kokila's bed; it showed the bakery job behind the music and led to a fair deal.

qa.q: Why was Kokila playing music so late?
qa.a: Kokila worked evenings at a bakery and used the music to stay awake to study, not to annoy Yamini.

grounding: An aunt recalls writing a conflict as a friend's story and from her roommate's side, and finding the reasons behind the late music.

passage: Fifteen minutes before the debate final, in a corridor full of noise, Nirmala and Trisha were barely speaking. Trisha had changed their opening argument without asking, and Nirmala felt ambushed. "She always has to be the star," Nirmala muttered, pacing by the water cooler. Then, with the clock ticking, she tried the trick their coach had taught them. If this were happening to my friend, what would I say? "Maybe she panicked." And from Trisha's seat? Nirmala pictured it: Trisha had heard the other team practising in the next room at lunch, using their exact opening. Nirmala walked back. "Did you hear them use our line?" Trisha's shoulders dropped with relief. "I tried to tell you, but you were at the registration desk." They had eight minutes left, and they used them together.

qa.q: How long before the final were they barely speaking?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala first think Trisha wanted to be the star?
qa.a: Nirmala felt ambushed and hurt that the opening had changed without asking, so it seemed to be about Trisha's character.

qa.q: What helped Nirmala under time pressure?
qa.a: Imagining it as a friend's problem and then from Trisha's seat, which led her to ask a real question instead of accusing.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel when Nirmala asked about the other team?
qa.a: Trisha felt relieved, her shoulders dropping, because she had been trying to explain.

grounding: Under time pressure, a student imagines a conflict as a friend's and from her teammate's seat, and finds the situational reason.

passage:
"Joel's late again," Rehana said, dropping her bag on her desk at 9:25. "Twenty minutes. He just doesn't take this job seriously."
Shalini looked up from her screen. "What time did you get in?"
"9:20. But the flyover was jammed; there was an accident near the signal."
"Joel takes the same flyover."
Rehana paused. "That's different. He's late a lot."
"He was late twice this month. You were late three times."
"Because of traffic!"
"Maybe his were too," Shalini said gently. "You're giving yourself the traffic and giving him the attitude."
Rehana sat down slowly. "Okay. That's annoyingly fair."
"Maybe ask him what's going on before the feedback meeting?"
"Yeah." Rehana opened her diary. "And maybe I'll ask how his commute is."

qa.q: Why was Rehana late, according to her?
qa.a: The flyover was jammed after an accident near the signal.

qa.q: How did Shalini seem to feel about Rehana's comment?
qa.a: Shalini seemed uneasy about the unfairness but spoke gently, not angrily, wanting Rehana to see the double standard.

qa.q: What does Shalini suggest before the feedback meeting, and why?
qa.a: Asking Joel what's going on, so the feedback rests on his situation rather than an assumed attitude.

qa.q: How does Rehana feel after Shalini points out the count?
qa.a: Rehana feels a bit caught out but accepts it, calling it annoyingly fair.

grounding: A colleague points out that a young manager excuses her own lateness by traffic but blames an employee's attitude.

passage: In my first job at the bank branch, I sat right outside our manager's cabin, so I heard things. One morning Naveen came in fifteen minutes late, and Mrs Grewal said loudly, "Some people have no discipline." The next week she arrived forty minutes late herself and told us, "The school bus broke down, I had to drop my son." Nobody said anything. I didn't either, at first. But when she started drafting Naveen's warning letter, I asked if I could mention something. "Ma'am, Naveen's mother has dialysis on Tuesdays. He's late on Tuesdays." She put the pen down. After a while she said, "I gave myself a reason and gave him a character." She called Naveen in, asked about Tuesdays and moved his start time. Later she said, "Amandeep, thank you for saying it."

qa.q: Why was Mrs Grewal forty minutes late?
qa.a: The school bus broke down and she had to drop her son.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep speak up about Naveen's Tuesdays?
qa.a: Amandeep felt uneasy that Naveen was about to be warned for something with a real reason, while Mrs Grewal excused her own lateness.

qa.q: What did Mrs Grewal do after hearing about Tuesdays, and why is it fairer?
qa.a: She asked Naveen about Tuesdays and moved his start time, giving him the same understanding she gave herself.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel when asked about Tuesdays instead of warned?
qa.a: Naveen would probably feel relieved and respected, with his mother's care recognised.

grounding: A young employee notices a manager excusing her own lateness but blaming a colleague's character, and speaks up.

passage:
HR partner's note, after the quarterly reviews, 12 July
In today's review, Parveen, one of our newest managers, described Anirban as having "a casual attitude" because he had arrived late to four morning meetings. Earlier in the same session, when I asked about her own two late arrivals, she had explained them as "the metro breakdowns that week." I asked her, gently, whether Anirban might have been on the same metro line. She checked: he was. She laughed at herself a little and said, "I gave myself the metro and gave him an attitude." She rewrote the comment as a question for their next one-to-one: "What's been making mornings hard?" I will suggest that all new managers check their feedback for the same pattern before submitting.

qa.q: How did Parveen explain her own late arrivals?
qa.a: The metro breakdowns that week.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel on finding Anirban used the same metro line?
qa.a: She felt a little embarrassed and laughed at herself, recognising the double standard.

qa.q: How did Parveen change her feedback, and why is it better?
qa.a: She turned the attitude comment into the question "What's been making mornings hard?", which is fair and curious.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel in the next one-to-one?
qa.a: Anirban would probably feel respected and able to explain, instead of being judged as casual.

grounding: An HR note records a new manager noticing she blamed traffic for herself but attitude for an employee, and rewriting her feedback.

subtype: It will not happen to me [Actor]
passage: The wind was picking up and the sky had gone yellow when Yogesh saw the last ripe mango at the top of the tree behind Nana's house. "I'm getting it," he said. His cousin Payal frowned. "The branches are wet. Ramu fell from that tree last year." "Ramu's clumsy. I won't fall. I never fall." He was halfway up when a gust shook the whole tree and his foot slipped off the wet bark. He hung by his arms, legs kicking. Payal screamed for Nana, who came running with the ladder and held it steady while Yogesh climbed down, shaking. Nana checked his scraped hands and sat him on the step. "Ramu thought he never fell too," Nana said quietly. The mango dropped by itself in the storm an hour later.

qa.q: Who fell from the tree last year?
qa.a: Ramu.

qa.q: Why was Yogesh so sure he wouldn't fall?
qa.a: He felt confident and a bit proud, believing falls happened to clumsy kids like Ramu, not to him.

qa.q: What went right after Yogesh slipped?
qa.a: Payal screamed for Nana straight away, and Nana brought the ladder, held it steady and checked his hands.

qa.q: What was it like for Payal to watch Yogesh slip?
qa.a: Payal was frightened, screaming for Nana, after warning him that the branches were wet.

grounding: A boy is sure he will not fall from a wet tree in rising wind, because falls happen to other children.

subtype: It will not happen to me [Actor]
passage: In their Kochi colony, Saurabh spent the whole week before the maths unit test playing football in the park until the streetlights came on. "Revise?" he laughed when Jomon asked. "People who fail are the ones who panic. I'll be fine. I'm always fine." Jomon stayed home with the fractions chapter. On the morning of the test, Saurabh looked at question three, adding fractions with different bottoms, and his mind went white. He tried to remember what Miss had said, then guessed. When the papers came back, he had 11 out of 25. He stared at the red number for a long time. "But I'm always fine," he said quietly. Jomon, who had 21, didn't say anything, just slid his fractions notes across the desk.

qa.q: What did Saurabh get in the test?
qa.a: 11 out of 25.

qa.q: Why was Saurabh sure he didn't need to revise?
qa.a: He felt carefree and certain that failing happens to people who panic, not to him.

qa.q: What small step could help Saurabh before the next test?
qa.a: Study the fractions chapter with Jomon's notes a few days before, instead of trusting that he'll always be fine.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel sliding his notes across?
qa.a: Jomon probably feels sorry for Saurabh and wants to help without rubbing it in.

grounding: A boy skips revision, sure that failing happens only to other people, and is stunned by his low mark.

passage:

"Ma'am checks," said Divyansh, his older brother, tying his shoes. "She caught three kids last week."
"They were stupid. They copied word for word. I'll change some words."
"That's what they did too."

"You got caught eating the laddoos at Diwali."

qa.q: Why does Eshaan believe he won't be caught?
qa.a: He feels confident and a bit cocky, sure that getting caught happens to other kids, not to him.

qa.q: What does Divyansh offer, and why is it a better plan?
qa.a: Help with the circuits question in the next ten minutes, so Eshaan can do his own homework instead of risking being caught copying.

qa.q: How does Divyansh see his brother's plan?
qa.a: Divyansh sees it as risky and familiar, since the three caught kids believed the same thing.

grounding: A boy is sure he will not be caught copying homework, because getting caught happens to other kids.

passage: Every morning Lalremsiami raced her bicycle down the steepest road in Aizawl to school, no helmet, hair flying, overtaking taxis on the bends. The school counsellor, Nazia ma'am, called her in after a teacher saw her skid at the gate. "You know Lalrina from Class 11 broke his collarbone on that road?" "He's reckless," Lalremsiami said. "I know what I'm doing. Nothing's going to happen to me." Nazia ma'am didn't lecture. She drew two circles on a page: "the rush now" and "what could happen later." "At your age the brain makes the first circle feel huge and the second feel far away. That's normal. It's also why we plan ahead." Lalremsiami looked at the circles. "Fine. What if I wear a helmet on the steep bit?" "Every bit," said Nazia ma'am, and handed her one from the sports room.

qa.q: What happened to Lalrina on that road?
qa.a: He broke his collarbone.

qa.q: Why does Lalremsiami believe nothing will happen to her?
qa.a: She feels thrilled and invincible on the fast ride, so injuries seem to belong to reckless others, not to someone who knows what she's doing.

qa.q: How did Nazia ma'am respond, and why did it work?
qa.a: She explained without lecturing how the brain makes the rush feel bigger than the risk at this age, then gave a practical step: a helmet for every ride.

qa.q: How might Nazia ma'am feel about the offer to wear a helmet on the steep bit?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and encouraged, but firm enough to ask for the helmet on every bit of the ride.

grounding: A teenage girl rides downhill without a helmet believing harm is for others, and a counsellor explains the pull of the rush and hands her a helmet.

passage:
Noor,
Don't start. I know you think vaping is dangerous. But it's only at weekends, and the stuff about lungs is for people who do it all day, not for me. I play football, I'm fit, I'll quit whenever I want. Honestly the only bad part was Papa finding the vape in my jacket yesterday. He didn't shout, which was worse. He just sat down and said we're going to meet the school counsellor together on Monday. He said something about my age, how the brain is wired to chase the good feeling now and push the later stuff away. I rolled my eyes. But I did look it up last night, and some of it was about people exactly like me.
Vaibhav

qa.q: When is Vaibhav meeting the school counsellor?
qa.a: On Monday, together with Papa.

qa.q: Why does Vaibhav believe vaping won't cause harm?
qa.a: Vaibhav feels fit, confident and in control, so the harms seem to belong to other people who do it all day.

qa.q: What is wise about Papa's response?
qa.a: He stayed calm, explained how the brain at this age chases the good feeling now, and arranged to see the school counsellor together.

qa.q: How might Noor feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Noor might feel worried but a little hopeful, noticing that Vaibhav looked it up and saw it described people like Vaibhav.

grounding: A teenager writes that vaping's harms are for other people, while a parent responds calmly and arranges a counsellor visit.

passage: Gurpreet, you asked why I stopped going to the canal. Okay. You know how in the monsoon everyone jumps from the old bridge? I did it every Sunday. People kept saying the current is strong after rain, a boy drowned there two years ago, all that. I honestly thought, that's other people. Kavitha is a good swimmer; nothing happens to me. Then last month the water was brown and fast and I jumped anyway. The current pulled me under the second arch. I came up, I don't even know how, and a fisherman dragged me to the bank. I walked home soaked and told Mummy everything that same evening. She held me for a long time, then went with me to the panchayat office to ask for a warning board. It's there now.

qa.q: Who dragged Kavitha to the bank?
qa.a: A fisherman.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha keep jumping even after hearing about the drowning?
qa.a: Kavitha felt confident and thrilled, believing danger was for other people and a good swimmer was safe.

qa.q: What did Kavitha and Mummy do after the near miss?
qa.a: Kavitha told Mummy everything that evening, and they went together to the panchayat office to ask for a warning board.

qa.q: What might Mummy have felt hearing the story?
qa.a: Mummy was probably terrified and deeply relieved, holding Kavitha for a long time before acting to protect others.

grounding: A teenager explains believing river danger was for others until a near miss, and the same-day family response that followed.

passage: When my offer letter from the design studio came in April, I planned for the best case only. The joining date said July 1. I gave up my PG in Pune, moved my things to Mumbai and signed a lease near the office, sure everything would go perfectly. Disha asked, "What if they push the date?" I laughed. "Other people's offers get delayed. Not mine." In June the studio emailed: joining postponed to October. Three months, no salary, a lease in my name. I sat on the floor of the empty flat and cried. It wasn't only the money. I felt stupid for never letting "what if" in. My parents helped, and I found freelance work. But now, whenever Zainab plans anything, there's a Plan B column.

qa.q: When was the joining date postponed to?
qa.a: October.

qa.q: Why did Zainab cry on the floor of the empty flat?
qa.a: Zainab felt shocked and foolish, because the plan had no room for a delay, so the setback hit much harder.

qa.q: What does Zainab do now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Adds a Plan B column to every plan, so hope stays but something is ready if things go wrong.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when the postponement came?
qa.a: Disha may have felt sad for Zainab, and perhaps wished the what-if question had been taken seriously.

grounding: A graduate recalls planning only for the best case after a job offer and being shaken when the joining date was pushed back.

passage:
Placement officer's note, final-year counselling, 5 March
Rukmini came in to confirm she will not sit for the remaining campus drives. She has one conditional offer from a start-up and is certain it will convert: "They loved me. It's basically done." She has also turned down her parents' suggestion to apply for the government exam "just in case." Her classmate Seema, who has a similar conditional offer, is still attending drives and has kept two backups. I told Rukmini her hope is reasonable and that the start-up may well confirm her. I also showed her last year's numbers: of eleven conditional offers from start-ups, four did not convert. She went quiet. We agreed she will attend two more drives, and we will meet again on 20 March.

qa.q: How many of last year's eleven conditional start-up offers did not convert?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: Why is Rukmini so sure the offer will convert?
qa.a: She feels hopeful and confident because the start-up loved her, so a failed offer seems like something that happens to others.

qa.q: What did the placement officer do that balanced hope with preparation?
qa.a: Agreed her hope was reasonable, showed last year's numbers, and agreed on two more drives as a backup.

qa.q: How does Seema's approach differ?
qa.a: Seema has a similar offer but keeps attending drives and has two backups, staying hopeful but prepared.

grounding: A placement officer records a graduate so sure of one offer that she was skipping all backup options.

passage:
Sunday, first week in Bengaluru
New job, new flat, new everything. I've already decided how this year goes: I'll save half my salary, go to the gym every morning, and Chinmay and I will make long distance work easily, because we're not like other couples. We'll talk every night.
Mumma asked on the phone if I had kept some money aside for emergencies. I said I'd start next month; nothing bad is going to happen in the first month.
Tonight Chinmay called at eleven, tired from his shift, and we argued about nothing for twenty minutes. First week. I'm sure it's just the first week.
Maybe I'll write down what I'd do if things don't go the way I think. Maybe tomorrow.
Gurleen

qa.q: What did Mumma ask about on the phone?
qa.a: Whether Gurleen had kept some money aside for emergencies.

qa.q: Why does Gurleen feel sure the year will go well?
qa.a: Gurleen feels hopeful and excited, believing bad things happen to other couples and other people, not in the first month.

qa.q: What small step could Gurleen take this week instead of maybe tomorrow?
qa.a: Write a simple backup plan for the year and talk it through with Mumma or someone experienced.

qa.q: What might Chinmay's side of the eleven o'clock call have been like?
qa.a: Chinmay was tired from his shift, so he may have felt drained and unable to meet the hope of a perfect nightly talk.

grounding: A graduate's diary shows expecting work, savings and a long-distance relationship to go better than average and putting off any backup plan.

passage:
March. Pema signed the lease for her small bakery counter in Gangtok with hope and a notebook. On one page: "Best case: busy by June." On the next: "If slower: evening tiffin orders. If the oven breaks: Raghav's bakery down the road will rent me time. Keep a cushion of savings untouched."
May. The oven broke two days before the tourist rush. Pema swore, then opened the notebook and called Raghav. For ten days she baked in his kitchen at dawn and carried trays up the hill.
July. Sales were slower than her best case, but the tiffin orders filled the gap. When a friend asked if the oven disaster had crushed her, Pema laughed. "It crushed my Tuesday. Not me. That's what the second page was for."

qa.q: Who rented Pema time in their kitchen?
qa.a: Raghav's bakery down the road.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when the oven broke?
qa.a: She was upset enough to swear, but steady, because the notebook already held a plan for exactly that.

qa.q: What made Pema's plan strong?
qa.a: She kept hope for the best case but wrote backups, like Raghav's kitchen and tiffin orders, so setbacks hit the plan, not her.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Pema's request?
qa.a: Raghav probably saw it as a sensible, agreed arrangement, which made helping easy.

grounding: Over a few months, a young baker keeps her hope but writes a second page of backups, so a broken oven upsets the plan and not her.

passage: Pallavi, you're starting your own practice, and everyone is either cheering or warning you. Let your Vinita mausi tell you what I did at twenty-five, when I left the firm to start my small architecture office. I was full of hope; I truly believed clients would come. But I also sat with my notebook and did three things. I kept some savings untouched, whatever happened. I kept one day a week teaching at the polytechnic, so there was always some pay coming in. And I wrote down: if no client by December, I'll take contract work and try again in a year. December came with only one small client. I took the contract work, and it stung my pride for a week. But it didn't break me. By the next summer, the office was full.

qa.q: How many days a week did Vinita teach at the polytechnic?
qa.a: One day a week.

qa.q: How did young Vinita feel when December came with only one client?
qa.a: Her pride stung for a week, but she felt steady rather than crushed, because the plan had already said what to do.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Vinita's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Writing down in advance what to do if no client came by December, so the setback changed her plan, not her belief in herself.

qa.q: How might the one small client have seen Vinita's office?
qa.a: The client probably saw a young, hopeful architect who took the work seriously.

grounding: An aunt recalls starting her own office full of hope while keeping savings, steady part-time work and a written plan B.

passage: By Friday night the forecast was certain: heavy rain on Saturday, the day of the open-air music festival Disha had spent six months planning. Kamal, her co-organiser, sat on the office floor surrounded by posters. "We're finished," he said. Disha opened her laptop. "We're inconvenienced." In January, full of hope, she had still booked the school hall as a backup, kept part of the budget aside and written a list: "If rain: move stage indoors, message all ticket holders, ask volunteers for umbrellas at the gate." At 10 p.m. the messages went out. On Saturday the hall was packed and steaming, people danced with wet hair, and the headline band played an extra song. Kamal shook his head. "You planned for rain in January?" "I hoped for sun," Disha said. "I planned for rain."

qa.q: What did Disha book as a backup?
qa.a: The school hall.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when the rain forecast was certain?
qa.a: She felt calm and steady, calling it an inconvenience rather than a disaster, because she was prepared.

qa.q: What did Disha do in January that saved the festival?
qa.a: She stayed hopeful but booked a backup hall, kept part of the budget aside and wrote a rain plan with clear steps.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel on Friday night compared with Saturday?
qa.a: On Friday he felt defeated, saying they were finished; on Saturday he was amazed that Disha had planned for rain in January.

grounding: Facing sudden rain, a young organiser's festival survives because she paired hope with a backup venue, a reserve and a written plan B.
